opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core insight behind RT-2 is actually pretty simple, and that's part of what makes it exciting. For a long time in robotics, we treated robot data as this special, precious thing that lived in its own world. You'd collect demonstrations, train a policy from scratch or from a vision backbone, and hope it generalized. But robot data is expensive and slow to collect, and no matter how hard we pushed, we were never going to get internet scale out of physical robots alone.

So the question with RT-2 was: what if we stop treating robot actions as fundamentally different from language? We took large vision-language models that had already been trained on enormous amounts of web data, image-text pairs, visual question answering, all of that, and we represented robot actions as just another sequence of tokens. Discretize the action space, turn it into text-like tokens, and now an action is something the model can "say," the same way it would answer a question about an image.

Then we co-fine-tuned on both the original web-scale vision-language data and our robot trajectory data. That co-training piece matters a lot, because if you only fine-tune on robot data you risk the model forgetting all the rich semantic knowledge it came in with. By keeping both in the mix, the model keeps its understanding of the world while learning how to ground that understanding in physical actions.

What really surprised us and got us excited was the emergent generalization. The robot data itself didn't contain concepts like "pick up the extinct animal" or "move the object to the picture of Taylor Swift" or "pick up the thing you could use as an improvised hammer." But the model could do those things, because that semantic knowledge came from the internet, and the robot data taught it the motor skills. So you get this transfer where web knowledge tells it *what* and *why*, and robot data tells it *how*.

I'd be careful not to overstate it, though. RT-2 didn't magically learn new physical skills it had never seen. If the robot data never included a certain kind of motion, the internet data won't teach that. The generalization was mostly semantic and visual, not about new low-level dexterity. And these are big models, so inference speed and running them in real time on a robot were real engineering challenges.

But philosophically, I think it was an important shift. It suggested robotics could ride the same wave as the rest of AI, where you inherit capabilities from foundation models instead of rebuilding everything from scratch. The robot data becomes this thin but crucial layer that connects all that knowledge to the physical world. And that changes how you think about scaling: you're not just asking how to collect more robot data, but how to best leverage everything these models already know.

r001.rationale: The response says web-trained semantic knowledge transfers to the robot, while robot data grounds that knowledge in physical actions.

r002.rationale: It identifies discretizing robot actions into text-like tokens so the model can produce actions as token sequences.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the core idea behind RT-2 is actually pretty simple to state, even if it took a lot of work to get right. We asked: what if you treat robot actions as just another language? Literally tokens, the same way a vision-language model handles words.

The backstory is that we'd spent years, going back to RT-1 and before, collecting robot-specific data. Tens of thousands of teleoperated episodes on real robots, which sounds like a lot until you compare it to the trillions of tokens that language models see, or the billions of image-text pairs that vision-language models train on. Robot data is slow and expensive to collect. You can't scrape it from the web. So there's this fundamental mismatch in scale.

Meanwhile, these big vision-language models, PaLI-X and PaLM-E in our case, already knew an enormous amount about the world. They knew what a Coke can looks like, they knew Taylor Swift's face, they knew that a banana is yellow and that trash goes in a bin. All of that is relevant to a robot. The question was how to get that knowledge into the robot's policy without throwing it away by training from scratch on our tiny robot dataset.

The trick was to represent actions as text. Each dimension of the action, the end-effector position, rotation, gripper state, we discretize into bins, and each bin maps to a token in the model's vocabulary. So a robot action just becomes a short string of numbers. And then you co-fine-tune: you train on the robot data and the original web-scale vision-language data at the same time. The model never stops being a vision-language model. It just learns that one more thing you can do with an image and an instruction is output an action string.

What we found is that the internet knowledge really does transfer. You get emergent capabilities where the robot can do things that never appeared in the robot data. "Move the apple to the Google logo," or "pick up the extinct animal" when there's a toy dinosaur on the table. The robot had never seen a dinosaur in its training data, but the VLM backbone knows what extinct means and what a dinosaur is, and that semantic understanding flows straight into the motor commands. You even see some rudimentary chain-of-thought, where the model reasons in text first and then emits the action.

I think the bigger lesson is that robotics doesn't have to solve the data problem alone. For a long time the field assumed we'd need to collect robot data at internet scale. RT-2 was evidence that you can borrow a lot of the heavy lifting from models trained on the internet, and the robot data mostly needs to teach the grounding, the mapping from understanding into physical action. Scale on the robot side still matters, which is partly what motivated things like Open X-Embodiment afterward, but the ratio looks a lot more tractable than it did before.

r001.rationale: It says internet-trained vision-language models transfer their world knowledge into robot policies, enabling capabilities absent from the robot data.

r002.rationale: It explains that RT-2 discretizes action dimensions into vocabulary tokens so the model can output robot actions as text.

astra-6.text:
The way I think about RT-2 is that we want to bring internet-scale knowledge into the robot’s decision-making process. A vision-language model already has a lot of useful knowledge about objects, language, and relationships in the world. But that doesn’t automatically mean it knows how to move a robot.

So the key idea is to represent robot actions as tokens, so that producing an action looks like another output task for the model. We train on robot demonstrations alongside vision-language tasks. The robot data teaches the model how to connect what it sees and what you ask for to physical actions, while the internet data provides a much broader foundation for interpreting the situation.

What’s exciting is that those two sources can work together. The robot can potentially understand a request involving a concept that never appeared explicitly in its robot demonstrations. But there’s an important distinction: broader semantic understanding doesn’t automatically give it a new physical skill. It still needs robot experience to ground that understanding in actions it can actually execute.

r001.rationale: The response says RT-2 brings internet-scale knowledge into robot decision-making and explains how internet data and robot demonstrations work together to support broader understanding.

r002.rationale: It identifies representing robot actions as tokens, making actions another model output task, as the mechanism connecting vision-language knowledge with robot actions.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about RT-2 is that we’re bringing robot actions into the same language that a vision-language model already uses. These models learn a lot from internet-scale images and text, but that knowledge doesn’t automatically tell a robot how to move. Robot demonstrations provide that grounding.

So we represent actions as tokens and co-fine-tune on both robot demonstrations and vision-language tasks. The model takes an image and an instruction, and instead of only producing a text answer, it can produce tokens that we decode into robot actions.

What’s exciting is that the robot data doesn’t have to teach every concept from scratch. If the model already has some understanding of what an extinct animal is, that can help it interpret an instruction like picking up the dinosaur toy, even if that particular instruction wasn’t in the robot training data. The demonstrations teach it how to execute the grasp; the broader training helps it understand what to grasp.

That doesn’t mean internet knowledge magically gives it new physical skills. It’s more that we can bring much richer semantic understanding into the skills the robot has learned.

r001.rationale: The response says internet-scale training provides semantic understanding that helps the robot interpret instructions, while robot demonstrations ground that understanding in learned skills.

r002.rationale: It identifies representing robot actions as tokens and decoding them into actions as the mechanism linking the model’s language-based representations to robotics.
